sections.h: Raphael and Tobit's last words on alms (Tobit 12 and 14)
sections.b: The book returns to alms at its two climaxes. Raphael's sermon repeats Tobit's charge: prayer with truth and alms with right deeds are better than wealth with wrongdoing, and "alms rescue from death, and they cleanse away every sin" (Tobit 12:8–9). Tobit's dying words give an example: Ahiqar's alms saved him from the death trap Nadab set, and Nadab fell into it himself (Tobit 14:10–11). Cyprian quoted Tobit 12:8–9 to urge Christians to give; Melanchthon's Apology answered that such texts praise the fruits of faith, not works that earn forgiveness.

Raphael tells the family that he brought the memorial of their prayers before the Lord's glory, that he was sent to test Tobit and to heal him and Sarah, and that he is "one of the seven angels who stand in attendance" before the Lord (Tobit 12:12–15). He only seemed to eat: "you were seeing a vision" (Tobit 12:19). Revelation knows the seven angels who stand before God (Revelation 8:2), and Gabriel says he "stands in the presence of God" (Luke 1:19). Raphael's use of a human name (Tobit 5:13) raised the question whether an angel may deceive, carded at Tobit 12.

sections.h: Angels and the memorial of prayer (Tobit 12:12)
sections.b: Raphael says, "I was the one who carried the memorial of your prayer before the Lord's glory" (Tobit 12:12), and the shorter Greek adds that the seven angels present the prayers of the saints (Tobit 12:15, see the variant there). The image matches Revelation 8:3–4, where an angel offers incense with the prayers of God's people, and Acts 10:4, where Cornelius's prayers and alms rise "as a memorial before God." Catholic and Orthodox teaching cite Tobit for the angels' part in prayer; Protestants hold that the passage does not teach praying to angels.

sections.h: The wedding night and Tobias's prayer (Tobit 7–8)
sections.b: Raguel gives Sarah to Tobias with a spoken formula and a written contract (Tobit 7:11–14), forerunners of the later Jewish ketubah. Before the couple sleep together Tobias prays, recalling God's making of Adam and Eve and saying he takes Sarah "not for sexual immorality, but in truth" (Tobit 8:5–8). The prayer is among the Catholic Lectionary's wedding readings, and the first English Prayer Book (1549) named Raphael, Tobias and Sarah in its marriage prayers. The question of what marriage is for, and whether the first nights should be kept for prayer, is carded at Tobit 8.

On the wedding night Tobias burns the fish's heart and liver; the smell drives the demon off, and it "fled up into the regions of Egypt"; Raphael goes after it and binds it there (Tobit 8:2–3). Egypt was famed in antiquity as a land of magic, and the binding of a demon by an angel recalls Raphael binding Azazel in 1 Enoch 10:4 and the binding of Satan in Revelation 20:2.

sections.h: God strikes and shows mercy (Tobit 11 and 13)
sections.b: When he sees again, Tobit blesses God and says, "He struck me, and look, I see my son Tobias!" (Tobit 11:14–15), and his hymn turns that into a rule for Israel: God "strikes, and he shows mercy" (Tobit 13:2, 13:5, 13:9). The words echo Deuteronomy 32:39 and 1 Samuel 2:6, and Raphael adds that Tobit was tested (Tobit 12:13–14). The book thus reads suffering as discipline that ends in mercy, close to Proverbs 3:11–12.

sections.b: Tobit's hymn sees Jerusalem rebuilt with sapphire and emerald, walls of precious stone, towers and battlements of gold, and streets set with red gems and stone of Ophir, while its houses cry "Hallelujah" (Tobit 13:16–18). The picture grows from Isaiah 54:11–12 and returns in Revelation 21:18–21 and 19:1–6. Whether that city is an earthly Jerusalem or the Church and the heavenly city is discussed on the Tobit 13 page; the cards on the thousand years (Revelation 20) and the promised land (Numbers 34) ask the wider question.

sections.h: Jerusalem in Tobit's hymn and testament
sections.b: Tobit, a northerner who once went alone to Jerusalem's feasts (Tobit 1:4–6), ends by addressing the city: it will be struck for its children's deeds but its tent will be rebuilt with joy, nations will come from far off bringing gifts, and those who love it will be happy (Tobit 13:9–14). His testament adds that after the exile the people will rebuild Jerusalem in splendor (Tobit 14:5).

sections.h: Scattered so that the nations may know (Tobit 13–14)
sections.b: Tobit's hymn gives the exile a purpose: Israel must thank God "in front of the nations," because God scattered them among the nations to show his greatness there (Tobit 13:3–4). If they turn to him with all their heart, he will turn to them and gather them (Tobit 13:5–6), as Deuteronomy 30:1–5 promised. His testament foretells the exile of Judah, the return and a lesser Temple, and then the gathering of all Israel (Tobit 14:4–7).

Tobit foretells that the Temple will be burned, then rebuilt, "but not like the first," until the appointed times are fulfilled; after that a glorious house will be built in Jerusalem (Tobit 14:4–5). The lesser second Temple recalls Ezra 3:12 and Haggai 2:3. Scholars use the passage to date the book: it knows the Second Temple but not its desecration in 167 BC.

Tobit believes that God's word against Nineveh will come true and sends his family to Media (Tobit 14:4, 14:8). Tobias lives to hear of the city's fall and rejoices over it (Tobit 14:15). Nineveh fell in 612 BC to the Medes and Babylonians; Sinaiticus names the conqueror "Achiacharus," which most read as Cyaxares of Media. Whether the prophet Tobit trusts is Nahum (Sinaiticus) or Jonah (Vaticanus) is discussed on the Tobit 14 page.

Tobit's last lesson retells the Story of Ahiqar: Nadab, raised by his uncle Ahiqar, tried to have him killed, but Ahiqar "came out into the light, while Nadab went down into darkness forever" (Tobit 14:10). The Aramaic Ahiqar, found among the Elephantine papyri of the 400s BC, shows that Jews knew the tale long before Tobit was written.

The man who buried the dead is buried with honor. Tobit is "buried with honor" in Nineveh (Tobit 14:1, 14:11), Tobias lays Anna to rest beside him as Tobit asked (Tobit 14:10, 14:12), and later buries Raguel and Edna in Ecbatana (Tobit 14:13). In Raguel's grave dug for Tobias and filled again before dawn (Tobit 8:9–18) the book plays the same theme for irony.
Tobit's hymn ends with the houses of Jerusalem crying "Hallelujah" and blessing God (Tobit 13:18), one of the few uses of the Hebrew word in a Greek book outside the Psalms before Revelation 19:1–6.

Tobit names sapphire, emerald, precious stone, gold, red gems and "stone of Ophir" for the rebuilt city (Tobit 13:16–17), a list built on Isaiah 54:11–12 and close to the foundations of Revelation 21:19–20.

The whole journey turns out to have been planned: Raphael was sent the moment Tobit and Sarah prayed (Tobit 3:16–17; Tobit 12:12–14), and he says, "it was not by any kindness of mine that I was with you; it was by God's will" (Tobit 12:18). Tobit's errand for money becomes the means of a marriage and a healing he could not have planned.
